prize_parts.citation: For the theory of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and its experimental realization in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: The Kane-Mele proposal of the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state, followed by Molenkamp's observation of protected edge transport in HgTe wells, is a complete chain from a theoretical idea to a discovery about nature. It gave condensed matter a new classification of phases through bulk-boundary topology, and nearly two decades of independent confirmation (transport, photoemission, many materials) make the interpretation stable. After reading my colleagues I am moving from the narrower B033 framing to B013: five of the eight openings credit Kane, Mele and Molenkamp or a close variant, and leaving Mele out of the theory credit, as my own B033 ballot did, is hard to defend since the Z2 paper is the conceptual core. Xue's quantum anomalous Hall realization is a real and distinct achievement, but it is better treated as a later development than bundled into this citation.
statement.case_against: The credit is compound. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's HgTe prediction is outside the credited names and was what made the Molenkamp experiment possible, and Hasan's three-dimensional photoemission work is a separate claim that this three-name set excludes. The 2016 prize on topological phases and phase transitions may also make a committee hesitate to return to topology so soon, even though that prize did not cover this line directly. Finally, quantum spin Hall and quantum anomalous Hall are separate discoveries, so the citation must stay disciplined to avoid overstating what the three credited laureates did.

responses.point: Ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a clean prediction-plus-discovery pair (Bistritzer-MacDonald, then Jarillo-Herrero) in a tunable system, reproduced in under a decade, with timing that looks ripe.
responses.response: I put the same candidate second and respect the argument, since the theory-then-experiment structure is as clean as in topology. My reservation is maturity and attribution. The superconducting mechanism is unresolved, and Eva Andrei's early scanning-probe evidence of flat bands is a credible competing claim that no three-name set resolves. Topological insulators have a stable interpretation and almost twice the confirmation time, so I would not call the cases equal. I do agree that the moire field is the strongest challenger and want it kept as the first alternative.

responses.point: Ranks optical lattice clocks first as an original, mature, two-name case with a pending redefinition of the second, and ranks topological insulators fourth.
responses.response: The two-name attribution for Katori and Ye is cleaner than anything in topology, and I accept that. Where I differ is on the weight of the discovery: a new organizing principle for electronic matter has, I think, wider scientific consequence than a gain in precision, however impressive. Precision timekeeping has also been recognized in 2005 and 2012. That is a judgement of weighting rather than a scientific objection, and the committee could reasonably prefer the clock case on cleanliness alone.

responses.point: Ranks the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp topological insulator case first, calling it a discovery in the prize sense, with a hard choice because Hasan and the BHZ theorists are left out.
responses.response: I agree with both the ranking and the difficulty she names. Where we may differ is how to handle the omissions. I would not stretch the credit to Hasan to fix them, because the three-dimensional photoemission work is a distinct achievement, and the BHZ prediction is not an available name. The honest course is a citation tied explicitly to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 concept, and I would rather accept that limit openly than blur it.

responses.point: Chooses Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan for the topological insulator case and drops Mele to stay within three names.
responses.response: I disagree on the credit. Hasan's 3D work is important, but dropping Mele removes one of the two authors of the foundational Z2 and quantum spin Hall paper to keep the three-dimensional realization, and that inverts the usual priority of the originating idea. With a three-person cap I would keep the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp chain, which maps to one coherent achievement, rather than mixing a 2D and a 3D discovery.

responses.point: Ranks the gamma-ray burst afterglow case first as a clean, instrument-driven discovery that settled the Galactic versus cosmological question and is arguably overdue.
responses.response: This is a strong, mature discovery and I ranked it fifth for exactly those reasons. My concern is attribution. Costa and Frontera on the X-ray side and Kulkarni on the optical and radio side are a defensible trio, but the optical discovery teams and the redshift measurements involved several people not in the credit set, and some key contributors have died. I would want that division resolved before putting it ahead of a case whose credit is at least mostly bounded by the supplied names.

responses.point: Places circuit QED third but warns that his proximity to the field may inflate his ranking, and notes the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits.
responses.response: I share the timing concern and think his own discount is the right one: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling makes a prize for the architecture of superconducting processors look too close in time. I do not think this reflects on the scientific merit of circuit QED, only on the question of when it should be recognized.

uncertainties: Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe prediction and Hasan's three-dimensional work can be set aside fairly given they are outside the three credited names.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases weighs against a further topology prize now.
Whether Eva Andrei's early flat-band evidence changes the balance for the twisted bilayer graphene alternative, and whether its superconducting mechanism needs to be settled first.
Whether the quantum anomalous Hall effect should be part of a later or separate topology prize rather than this citation.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My professional connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) are in string theory and gravity and none of the credited candidates is among them. I note only that I am a formal theorist and may tend to favor a concept with a clean theoretical core.
